primary_cause: Q4 earnings miss + COVID oil demand fears
secondary_factors: Raised dividend 38% and expanded buybacks to $25B but market focused on miss
store_description: ConocoPhillips fell after reporting Q4 2019 results on Feb. 4. Adjusted EPS $0.76 versus roughly $0.81 expected with GAAP EPS of $0.65 while year-over-year earnings declined sharply. Even though COP boosted its dividend to $0.42/share and expanded buybacks to $25B the market focused on the earnings shortfall and weaker profit profile.

primary_cause: Pre-earnings positioning ahead of Feb 6 Q4 report
secondary_factors: Still unprofitable regulatory overhang around driver classification
store_description: Uber's Feb. 5 decline appears to have been mostly a pre-earnings move rather than a reaction to a fresh company headline. Uber was set to report Q4 on Feb. 6 and investors were already bracing for another large loss in a stock still under scrutiny for profitability and regulatory risk. The next day Uber reported $4.1B revenue $18.1B gross bookings and a $1.10B GAAP net loss.

primary_cause: No stock-specific catalyst found. High-multiple software valuation pressure
secondary_factors: Q4 reported Jan 29 already absorbed
store_description: Could not verify a fresh ServiceNow-specific event in the three days before the Feb. 5 decline. The most likely explanation is a valuation-led pullback in high-multiple software stocks after earnings season rather than a new filing guidance change or analyst action directly tied to ServiceNow that day.

primary_cause: COVID China supply chain and demand fears hitting semis
secondary_factors: Dec earnings had been constructive signaling 2020 recovery
store_description: Micron's Feb. 7 weakness does not appear tied to a fresh company announcement. The best explanation is early COVID supply-chain and China-demand anxiety hitting semiconductor names which mattered for Micron because investors were evaluating how disruptions in China could affect memory demand and manufacturing even though December results had pointed to a recovery.

primary_cause: Post-earnings digestion plus COVID China smartphone fears
secondary_factors: Reported Feb 5 after close with mixed reaction
store_description: Qualcomm's Feb. 7 drop does not line up with a clearly identifiable new negative company event. The most plausible read is a post-earnings pullback amplified by coronavirus fears around China smartphone demand and production which weighed on handset and semiconductor names broadly in early February.

primary_cause: Macro transport sector concern tied to COVID trade volume risk
secondary_factors: Post-earnings digestion from late-January results
store_description: UPS's Feb. 7 decline appears to have been driven mainly by growing concern about global shipping demand and supply-chain disruption from the coronavirus outbreak not by a fresh UPS-specific announcement. With transport names acting as economic barometers UPS was pressured as investors began pricing in weaker cross-border volume and industrial activity.

primary_cause: Weak Q3 forward guidance after fiscal Q2 results
secondary_factors: Enterprise networking demand softening concerns
store_description: Cisco fell after reporting fiscal Q2 revenue of $12.0B and non-GAAP EPS of $0.77 but the bigger issue was a soft Q3 outlook. Management guided to a 1.5% to 3.5% y/y revenue decline and $0.79 to $0.81 non-GAAP EPS reinforcing concerns about slowing enterprise and networking demand.

primary_cause: Semiconductor equipment sector de-risking on COVID China fab fears
secondary_factors: First trading day after Presidents Day. Group had run up sharply
store_description: Lam Research's Feb. 18 decline appears to have been mostly a sector move not a reaction to a fresh Lam-specific announcement. Semiconductor-equipment stocks were increasingly pressured by fears that the coronavirus outbreak would disrupt Chinese manufacturing fab spending timing and the electronics supply chain.

primary_cause: Earnings reaction on fiscal Q3 results day
secondary_factors: Early COVID elective procedure uncertainty beginning
store_description: Medtronic fell on the day it reported fiscal Q3 2020 results. The company posted $7.7B in revenue up 2.3% reported and 2.6% organic. The drop appears to have been an earnings-driven reaction rather than a separate news event.

primary_cause: Macro financial sector pressure from falling yields and COVID fears
secondary_factors: Banks vulnerable as investors rotated away from cyclicals
store_description: Morgan Stanley's Feb. 20 decline does not appear to be linked to a fresh company headline. The most likely driver was sector pressure on financials as Treasury yields fell and coronavirus fears increased which hurt sentiment around banks and other economically sensitive names.

primary_cause: Semiconductor sector COVID selloff. Reported Feb 13 initially traded well
secondary_factors: Post-earnings profit-taking in high-beta semi winner
store_description: Nvidia's Feb. 21 selloff looks primarily like a sector-wide semiconductor de-risking move rather than a fresh Nvidia-specific miss or warning. Investors were increasingly worried that the coronavirus outbreak would hit China demand and electronics supply chains and richly valued chip leaders like Nvidia were sold aggressively as that risk was repriced.

primary_cause: Transport economic growth fears tied to COVID
secondary_factors: Oil freight and global trade expectations turning less favorable
store_description: UPS's Feb. 21 decline appears to have been driven mainly by macro fears about weaker shipping and trade activity as coronavirus spread globally not by a fresh company-specific announcement. Transport stocks were increasingly treated as a read-through on global growth risk.

primary_cause: Rate-sensitive financial pressure from falling Treasury yields
secondary_factors: Schwab earnings model more rate-sensitive than many other financials
store_description: Charles Schwab's Feb. 21 drop does not line up with a fresh company-specific catalyst. The most likely explanation is rate-sensitive financial pressure as investors rushed into Treasuries on coronavirus concerns falling yields worsened the outlook for Schwab's net interest revenue.

primary_cause: Semiconductor sector COVID fears. Memory names cyclical
secondary_factors: Macro demand fears hit memory harder than broad market
store_description: Micron's Feb. 21 decline seems to have been driven by broad semiconductor selling tied to coronavirus fears not by a fresh Micron-specific headline. Investors were increasingly worried about the impact of China shutdowns on electronics demand memory pricing and the supply chain.

primary_cause: Broad tech risk-off move not Microsoft-specific
secondary_factors: Actual COVID warning came Feb 26 for More Personal Computing segment
store_description: Microsoft's Feb. 21 decline appears to have been a broad risk-off move in large-cap tech not a reaction to a fresh company announcement. The company's actual coronavirus-related warning came nearly a week later when Microsoft said its More Personal Computing unit would miss prior guidance because the China supply chain was recovering more slowly than expected.

primary_cause: Sector-wide semi equipment selloff on COVID China fears
secondary_factors: Profit-taking after strong run in equipment names
store_description: Lam Research fell on Feb. 21 as investors sold semiconductor-equipment stocks on mounting coronavirus supply-chain and China-demand concerns. No fresh Lam-specific release or analyst action verified so this looks mainly like a sector de-risking move.

primary_cause: High-beta semiconductor selloff on COVID risk. 7% drop larger than group
secondary_factors: Valuation and profit-taking amplified magnitude versus peers
store_description: AMD's 7% drop on Feb. 21 does not appear tied to a fresh AMD-specific miss guidance cut or filing. The move is best explained as an aggressive derating of high-beta semiconductor stocks as investors priced in coronavirus-related risks to China demand manufacturing and the broader electronics supply chain.

primary_cause: Sector-wide semi equipment risk-off move
secondary_factors: Investors looking through recent strong results focusing on COVID risk
store_description: Applied Materials' Feb. 21 decline does not appear to have been driven by a fresh company-specific negative. Instead the stock was caught in the broader semiconductor-equipment selloff as the market repriced coronavirus-related risks to manufacturing supply chains and future wafer-fab spending.

primary_cause: Feb 24 COVID panic day (S&P -3%+) overwhelmed same-day earnings
secondary_factors: Fiscal Q2 results not obviously bad. Q3 non-GAAP EPS guided $5.90-5.95. FY reiterated
store_description: Intuit fell on the same day it reported fiscal Q2 results but the release itself was not obviously disastrous. The company guided Q3 non-GAAP EPS to $5.90-$5.95 and reiterated full-year revenue of $7.44B-$7.54B and non-GAAP EPS of $7.50-$7.60. The more likely explanation is that INTU was dragged down by the Feb. 24 coronavirus-driven market break when the S&P 500 fell more than 3% as investors reacted to the spread in Italy and South Korea.

primary_cause: COVID elective procedure volume fears on Feb 24 panic day
secondary_factors: High valuation medtech. Later confirmed procedure volumes fell sharply
store_description: Intuitive Surgical's Feb. 24 drop does not appear tied to a new company filing or guidance change. Investors began to price in procedure-volume risk from the spreading coronavirus outbreak which was particularly relevant to Intuitive because its da Vinci business depends heavily on hospital scheduling and elective surgeries. Later company commentary confirmed that procedure volumes did fall sharply as COVID spread.
